points.title: Sub-atomic particles
points.content: Proton: relative mass 1, charge +1, in nucleus. Neutron: relative mass 1, charge 0, in nucleus. Electron: relative mass 1/1840, charge −1, outside nucleus.

points.title: Mass spectrometer steps
points.content: 1. Vaporisation → 2. Ionisation (electron bombardment) → 3. Acceleration → 4. Deflection (magnetic field) → 5. Detection. Ions with same m/z arrive together.

points.title: Calculating Ar from mass spectrum
points.content: Ar = Σ(isotopic mass × relative abundance) / Σ(relative abundances). Multiply each peak's m/z by its height/%, sum all, divide by total %.

points.title: Electron sub-shells order
points.content: Fill in order of increasing energy: 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p, 5s, 4d... Note: 4s fills before 3d but empties before 3d in transition metals.

points.title: Hund's rule
points.content: Electrons occupy orbitals of the same energy (degenerate orbitals) singly before pairing. All single electrons have parallel spins.

points.title: Ionisation energy trends
points.content: Across a period: generally increases (increasing nuclear charge). Down a group: decreases (increased shielding, greater distance from nucleus). Exceptions: slight drop at Group 3 (2p vs 2s) and Group 6 (pairing in 2p).

points.title: Emission spectrum of hydrogen
points.content: Electrons fall from higher to lower energy levels, releasing photons. Lyman series (UV): n→1. Balmer series (visible): n→2. Paschen series (IR): n→3. ΔE = hf = hc/λ.

points.title: Evidence for shells from IE
points.content: Large jumps in successive ionisation energies indicate change of shell. The jump position shows how many electrons are in the outer shell.

points.title: Shapes of orbitals
points.content: s orbital: spherical. p orbital: two lobes (dumbbell), three p orbitals (px, py, pz) perpendicular to each other. d orbitals: five d orbitals with more complex shapes.

points.title: Shielding effect
points.content: Inner electrons repel outer electrons, reducing the effective nuclear charge felt by outer electrons. More inner shells = more shielding = lower IE.

points.title: Mole calculations
points.content: n = m/M (mass/molar mass). n = V/24 (gas volume in dm³ at RTP). n = cV (concentration × volume in dm³). c = n/V.

points.title: Empirical vs molecular formula
points.content: Empirical = simplest ratio. Molecular = actual number of atoms. Molecular formula = n × empirical formula, where n = Mr(molecular) / Mr(empirical).

points.title: % composition by mass
points.content: % element = (n × Ar of element / Mr of compound) × 100%. Conversely: divide % by Ar, find simplest ratio → empirical formula.

points.title: Ideal gas equation
points.content: pV = nRT. Use SI units: p in Pa, V in m³, T in K, R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. At RTP (25°C, 100 kPa): Vm = 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹. At STP (0°C, 100 kPa): Vm = 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹.

points.title: Limiting reagent method
points.content: 1. Calculate moles of each reactant. 2. Divide by stoichiometric coefficient. 3. Smaller value = limiting reagent. 4. Calculate product from limiting reagent moles.

points.title: Percentage yield
points.content: % yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) × 100%. Theoretical yield calculated from limiting reagent via stoichiometry.

points.title: Atom economy
points.content: Atom economy = (Mr of desired product(s) / total Mr of all products) × 100%. Higher atom economy = greener process (less waste).

points.title: Concentration calculations
points.content: Molarity c (mol dm⁻³) = n/V. Dilution: c₁V₁ = c₂V₂. Titration: at equivalence point, moles acid from one source are stoichiometrically equivalent to base.

points.title: Volumetric analysis procedure
points.content: 1. Pipette known volume of one solution. 2. Add indicator. 3. Burette with other solution. 4. Titrate to endpoint. 5. Repeat for concordant results (within 0.1 cm³). 6. Calculate moles, then unknown concentration.

points.title: VSEPR shapes
points.content: 2 bp: linear (180°). 3 bp: trigonal planar (120°). 4 bp: tetrahedral (109.5°). 3 bp + 1 lp: pyramidal (~107°). 2 bp + 2 lp: bent/V-shaped (~104.5°). 5 bp: trigonal bipyramidal. 6 bp: octahedral (90°).

points.title: Effect of lone pairs on bond angles
points.content: Lone pairs occupy more space than bonding pairs, reducing bond angles. Each lone pair reduces angles by ~2.5°. Order of repulsion: lp-lp > lp-bp > bp-bp.

points.title: Hybridisation summary
points.content: sp³: tetrahedral (methane, water, ammonia). sp²: trigonal planar, one unhybridised p orbital for π bond (ethene, BF₃). sp: linear, two unhybridised p orbitals for two π bonds (ethyne, CO₂, BeCl₂).

points.title: Electronegativity and bond polarity
points.content: If ΔEN > 1.7: ionic. If 0.4 < ΔEN < 1.7: polar covalent. If ΔEN < 0.4: non-polar covalent. Pauling values: F(4.0) > O(3.5) > N(3.0) > Cl(3.0) > Br(2.8) > C(2.5) > H(2.1).

points.title: Intermolecular forces comparison
points.content: Hydrogen bonds (~20 kJ/mol) > Permanent dipole-dipole (~2-5 kJ/mol) > Van der Waals/London (depends on size). VdW increases with Mr (more electrons = larger temporary dipoles).

points.title: Conditions for hydrogen bonding
points.content: Must have: H bonded directly to N, O, or F in one molecule AND a lone pair on N, O, or F in another molecule. Examples: H₂O (2 H-bonds per molecule), NH₃, HF, DNA base pairs.

points.title: Properties of ionic compounds
points.content: High melting/boiling points (strong ionic bonds). Conduct electricity when molten or dissolved (mobile ions). Hard but brittle. Soluble in polar solvents.

points.title: Giant covalent structures
points.content: Diamond: 4 C-C bonds, tetrahedral, very hard, no electrical conduction. Graphite: 3 C-C bonds, layers, delocalized π electrons (conducts), lubricant. SiO₂: giant lattice, very hard, high mp.

points.title: Sigma and pi bonds
points.content: Single bond = 1 σ bond. Double bond = 1 σ + 1 π bond. Triple bond = 1 σ + 2 π bonds. Rotation is possible around σ bonds but NOT around π bonds (restricted rotation in C=C causes geometric isomerism).

points.title: Metallic bonding and properties
points.content: Positive metal ions in a sea of delocalised electrons. High electrical/thermal conductivity (mobile electrons). Malleable/ductile (layers slide). High melting point (strong attraction). Increases with more delocalised electrons and smaller ion radius.

points.title: Kinetic theory assumptions
points.content: Molecules are point masses with negligible volume. No intermolecular forces. Collisions are perfectly elastic. Average KE ∝ absolute temperature (T in Kelvin). Molecules move in random directions.

points.title: Real vs ideal gas deviations
points.content: At high pressure: real gas volume > ideal (repulsive forces) or < ideal (attractive forces dominate). At low temperature: attractive forces significant → real gas volume < ideal. Ideal behaviour: high T, low P.

points.title: Types of crystal structures
points.content: Ionic (NaCl): high mp, conducts when molten/dissolved. Giant covalent (SiO₂, diamond): very high mp, no conduction. Simple molecular (ice, I₂): low mp, no conduction. Metallic (Fe, Cu): high mp, conducts.

points.title: Allotropes of carbon
points.content: Diamond: sp³, tetrahedral, hardest natural substance, insulator. Graphite: sp², layered, conductor (delocalised electrons), lubricant. Buckminsterfullerene (C₆₀): spherical, molecular, used in nanotechnology.

points.title: Effect of structure on melting point
points.content: Giant structures (ionic, covalent, metallic) have high melting points (must break many bonds). Simple molecular structures have low melting points (only overcome weak Van der Waals). Larger molecules have higher melting points (more VdW).

points.title: Standard conditions
points.content: Temperature: 298 K (25°C). Pressure: 100 kPa (1 bar). Concentration: 1 mol dm⁻³ for solutions. All substances in their standard states.

points.title: Hess's Law application
points.content: ΔHreaction = ΣΔHf°(products) − ΣΔHf°(reactants). OR use a two-step Hess cycle: route 1 (direct) = route 2 (via intermediates). ΔHf° of elements in standard states = 0.

points.title: Bond enthalpy calculations
points.content: ΔH = Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed). Bonds broken: endothermic (+). Bonds formed: exothermic (−). Mean bond enthalpies give approximate values; exact values require specific compound data.

points.title: Calorimetry calculation
points.content: q = mcΔT (m = mass of solution in g, c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ for water, ΔT = temperature change). ΔH = −q/n (negative sign: exothermic when T rises). Limitations: heat loss to surroundings, incomplete reaction.

points.title: Enthalpy profile diagrams
points.content: Exothermic: products lower than reactants, ΔH < 0. Endothermic: products higher than reactants, ΔH > 0. Activation energy (Ea) is always positive. Catalyst lowers Ea but does NOT change ΔH.

points.title: Definitions of standard enthalpies
points.content: ΔHf°: forming 1 mol compound from elements in standard states. ΔHc°: completely burning 1 mol substance. ΔHat°(element): forming 1 mol gaseous atoms from element. ΔHat°(compound): forming gaseous atoms from 1 mol compound.

points.title: Oxidation number rules
points.content: 1. Free element = 0. 2. Monatomic ion = ionic charge. 3. O = −2 (except in peroxides −1, OF₂ +2). 4. H = +1 (except metal hydrides −1). 5. Sum = overall charge of species.

points.title: Balancing half-equations
points.content: 1. Balance atoms other than O and H. 2. Balance O by adding H₂O. 3. Balance H by adding H⁺. 4. Balance charge by adding e⁻. 5. Combine half-equations (multiply to equalise electrons). Acidic conditions: use H⁺/H₂O. Alkaline: use OH⁻/H₂O.

points.title: Oxidising/reducing agent identification
points.content: The species that gains electrons (is reduced) is the oxidising agent. The species that loses electrons (is oxidised) is the reducing agent. OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain.

points.title: Common oxidising agents
points.content: MnO₄⁻ (KMnO₄): Mn +7 → +2 (acidic) or +4. Cr₂O₇²⁻: Cr +6 → +3. H₂O₂: O −1 → −2. Cl₂: Cl 0 → −1. O₂: O 0 → −2. Fe³⁺: Fe +3 → +2.

points.title: Common reducing agents
points.content: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺. SO₂/SO₃²⁻ → SO₄²⁻. I⁻ → I₂. H₂O₂ → O₂ (also oxidising agent). Metals (e.g. Fe, Zn) → metal ions.

points.title: Disproportionation examples
points.content: Cl₂ + H₂O → HCl + HClO (Cl: 0 → −1 and +1). H₂O₂ → H₂O + O₂ (O: −1 → −2 and 0). Cu⁺ → Cu + Cu²⁺.

points.title: Writing Kc expressions
points.content: For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD: Kc = [C]^c × [D]^d / ([A]^a × [B]^b). Pure solids and liquids are NOT included (activity = 1). Units depend on Δn = (c+d) − (a+b).

points.title: Kp expressions and calculations
points.content: Kp = Π p(products) / Π p(reactants). Partial pressure p = mole fraction × total pressure. Mole fraction = n(gas) / n(total gas). Kp units: Pa raised to Δn.

points.title: Effect of changes on equilibrium (Le Chatelier)
points.content: Increase concentration of reactant → shift right (more products). Increase pressure (gas) → shift to side with fewer moles of gas. Increase temperature → shift in endothermic direction. Catalyst → no effect on position, only reaches equilibrium faster.

points.title: Kc and temperature
points.content: Increasing T shifts equilibrium endothermic direction. If forward reaction is exothermic: Kc decreases with increasing T. If forward reaction is endothermic: Kc increases with increasing T. Catalyst does NOT affect Kc.

points.title: Haber process optimisation
points.content: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹. High pressure → higher yield (fewer moles gas on right). Low temperature → higher yield (exothermic). But low T is slow → compromise: 450°C, 200 atm, Fe catalyst.

points.title: Industrial equilibria trade-offs
points.content: Compromise conditions balance yield and rate. Very high P is expensive (engineering costs). Catalyst increases rate without affecting yield. Economic viability requires continuous process with recycling of unreacted gases.

points.title: Factors affecting rate
points.content: Temperature (↑T → ↑rate; more particles exceed Ea, more frequent collisions). Concentration (↑c → ↑rate; more frequent collisions). Pressure (gases: ↑P → ↑rate). Surface area (solids: ↑SA → ↑rate). Catalyst (lower Ea → ↑rate).

points.title: Collision theory
points.content: Reaction occurs when: 1. Particles collide. 2. With sufficient energy (≥ Ea). 3. With correct orientation. Rate ∝ frequency of successful collisions.

points.title: Boltzmann distribution and temperature
points.content: At higher T: curve shifts right, peak moves right and down, area under curve is same (total particles unchanged). Area to right of Ea increases significantly → much greater fraction of molecules have energy ≥ Ea.

points.title: Determining reaction order from data
points.content: Zero order: rate independent of [A], [A] vs t is linear. First order: rate ∝ [A], ln[A] vs t is linear, constant t½. Second order: rate ∝ [A]², 1/[A] vs t is linear, t½ increases with decreasing [A].

points.title: Rate equations and units
points.content: rate = k[A]^m[B]^n. Overall order = m + n. Units of k: for zero order: mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹; first order: s⁻¹; second order: dm³ mol⁻¹ s⁻¹. Doubling [A]: if 1st order → rate × 2; if 2nd order → rate × 4.

points.title: Catalysis mechanisms
points.content: Heterogeneous: reactants adsorb onto catalyst surface (active sites), bonds weaken, reaction occurs, products desorb. Example: Fe in Haber process. Homogeneous: catalyst in same phase, forms intermediate. Example: Mn²⁺ catalysing H₂O₂ decomposition.

points.title: Half-life of first order reactions
points.content: t½ = ln 2 / k = 0.693 / k. Constant half-life regardless of initial concentration. If t½ doubles when [A] halves → NOT first order (second order has increasing t½).

points.title: Period 3 structure and bonding
points.content: Na, Mg, Al: metallic lattices. Si: giant covalent. P₄, S₈, Cl₂, Ar: simple molecular. This explains the trend in melting points: increases Na→Si, then drops sharply P→Ar.

points.title: Period 3 oxide reactions with water
points.content: Na₂O: strongly alkaline (Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH). MgO: weakly alkaline. Al₂O₃: amphoteric (reacts with both acid and alkali). SiO₂: insoluble (giant covalent). P₄O₁₀: weakly/strongly acidic. SO₂: weakly acidic. SO₃: strongly acidic. Cl₂O₇: very strongly acidic.

points.title: Period 3 chlorides with water
points.content: NaCl: neutral solution (ionic, dissociates). MgCl₂: slightly acidic. AlCl₃: acidic (Al³⁺ hydrolyses). SiCl₄: fumes of HCl, forms SiO₂ + HCl. PCl₃: H₃PO₃ + HCl. PCl₅: H₃PO₄ + HCl. SCl₂: very acidic.

points.title: Trends in atomic radius
points.content: Decreases across a period (increasing Zeff, same shell). Increases down a group (more electron shells, increased shielding). Transition metals: similar radii due to shielding of d electrons.

points.title: Trends in electronegativity
points.content: Increases across a period (increasing Zeff). Decreases down a group (increased shielding and atomic radius). Most electronegative: F (4.0). Pauling scale values used in A-level.

points.title: Ionisation energy anomalies in Period 2
points.content: Drop from Be to B: B has one 2p electron, easier to remove than 2s. Drop from N to O: O has a paired 2p electron (extra repulsion), easier to remove than N's unpaired electron.

points.title: Reactions of Group 2 metals
points.content: With O₂: 2M + O₂ → 2MO (Mg burns brilliantly white; Ba forms BaO₂). With water: M + 2H₂O → M(OH)₂ + H₂ (Mg reacts slowly; Ca–Ba react vigorously). With dilute acids: M + H₂SO₄ → MSO₄ + H₂.

points.title: Solubility trends
points.content: Hydroxides: Mg(OH)₂ sparingly soluble → Ba(OH)₂ soluble (increases down group). Sulfates: MgSO₄ soluble → BaSO₄ insoluble (decreases down group). CaSO₄ sparingly soluble (scale in pipes).

points.title: Thermal stability of carbonates
points.content: MCO₃ → MO + CO₂. Stability increases down group (Mg easier to decompose; BaCO₃ requires higher T). Small, highly charged cation (Mg²⁺) polarises CO₃²⁻ more → destabilises → decomposes at lower T.

points.title: Uses of Group 2 compounds
points.content: Ca(OH)₂ (slaked lime): neutralises acidic soils, flue gas desulfurisation. CaCO₃ (limestone): building material, neutralisation. BaSO₄: barium meal (X-ray contrast agent, insoluble so non-toxic). MgO: refractory (high mp).

points.title: Flame colours
points.content: Mg: no characteristic colour (bright white light). Ca: brick-red. Sr: crimson. Ba: green.

points.title: Physical properties trends
points.content: Boiling point: F₂ < Cl₂ < Br₂ < I₂ (increases with Mr, stronger VdW forces). State at RTP: F₂ and Cl₂ (gases), Br₂ (liquid), I₂ (solid). Colour: F₂ (pale yellow), Cl₂ (green-yellow), Br₂ (red-brown), I₂ (dark grey/purple vapour).

points.title: Halogen displacement reactions
points.content: A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one from its salt. Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2Cl⁻. Cl₂ + 2I⁻ → I₂ + 2Cl⁻. Br₂ + 2I⁻ → I₂ + 2Br⁻. F₂ displaces all; I₂ displaces none. Use organic solvent to identify halogen by colour.

points.title: Reactions with NaOH
points.content: Cold dilute NaOH: Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O (bleach/disinfectant). Hot concentrated NaOH: 3Cl₂ + 6NaOH → 5NaCl + NaClO₃ + 3H₂O. Both are disproportionation reactions.

points.title: Testing for halide ions
points.content: Add dilute HNO₃ (to remove CO₃²⁻, SO₃²⁻ interferences), then AgNO₃(aq). AgCl: white precipitate, soluble in dilute NH₃. AgBr: cream precipitate, soluble in concentrated NH₃. AgI: yellow precipitate, insoluble in NH₃.

points.title: Hydrogen halide bond strengths
points.content: HF > HCl > HBr > HI (bond enthalpy decreases, acid strength increases). HF is a weak acid (strong H-bond). HCl, HBr, HI are strong acids. HI is the strongest reducing agent (I⁻ can reduce H₂SO₄ to H₂S).

points.title: Reactions of halide ions with H₂SO₄
points.content: NaCl + H₂SO₄ → NaHSO₄ + HCl (only acid-base, Cl⁻ not strong enough to reduce H₂SO₄). NaBr + H₂SO₄ → fumes of HBr, also some Br₂ and SO₂. NaI + H₂SO₄ → HI, I₂, H₂S, S (more vigorous reduction due to stronger reducing power of I⁻).

points.title: Haber Process
points.content: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹. Conditions: 450°C, 200 atm, iron catalyst with K₂O/Al₂O₃ promoter. ~15% yield per pass; unreacted gases recycled. Trade-off: lower T → higher yield but slower rate.

points.title: Ostwald Process (HNO₃ manufacture)
points.content: 1. 4NH₃ + 5O₂ → 4NO + 6H₂O (Pt/Rh catalyst, 900°C). 2. 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂. 3. 4NO₂ + O₂ + 2H₂O → 4HNO₃.

points.title: Contact Process (H₂SO₄ manufacture)
points.content: 1. S + O₂ → SO₂. 2. 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ (V₂O₅ catalyst, 450°C, 1 atm). 3. SO₃ + H₂SO₄ → H₂S₂O₇ (oleum). 4. H₂S₂O₇ + H₂O → 2H₂SO₄. Cannot add water directly to SO₃ (too vigorous, acidic mist).

points.title: Environmental issues
points.content: SO₂: causes acid rain (2SO₂ + O₂ + 2H₂O → 2H₂SO₄); removed by FGD using CaCO₃ or Ca(OH)₂. NOₓ: from vehicle engines, contributes to acid rain and photochemical smog. Catalytic converters: 2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂ (Pt/Rh).

points.title: Properties of ammonia
points.content: Weak base (pKb ~4.7). Reacts with acids: NH₃ + HCl → NH₄Cl. Ligand (lone pair on N): forms [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺ (deep blue) with Cu²⁺ after dissolving Cu(OH)₂ precipitate. Test: moist red litmus turns blue.

points.title: Types of structural isomers
points.content: Chain isomers: different carbon skeletons. Position isomers: same functional group in different positions. Functional group isomers: same formula, different functional groups (e.g. alcohol vs ether, aldehyde vs ketone).

points.title: Geometric isomerism conditions
points.content: Requires: C=C double bond (or ring) AND two different groups on each carbon of the double bond. Cis: same groups on same side. Trans: same groups on opposite sides. Note: if either carbon has two identical groups, no geometric isomerism.

points.title: Optical isomerism
points.content: Requires a chiral carbon (4 different groups). Two enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images. Racemic mixture (racemate): equal amounts of both enantiomers, optically inactive. Plane-polarised light: (+) enantiomer rotates clockwise; (−) anticlockwise.

points.title: Reaction mechanisms types
points.content: Free radical substitution (alkanes + Cl₂/Br₂, UV). Electrophilic addition (alkenes). Nucleophilic substitution (halogenoalkanes). Electrophilic substitution (benzene). Nucleophilic addition (carbonyls). Addition-elimination / condensation.

points.title: Drawing mechanisms
points.content: Use curly arrows to show electron pair movement. Arrow starts from electron source (bond or lone pair) → goes to electron sink (electrophilic centre). Show all intermediates (carbocations, carbanions, radicals). For ionic mechanisms: show charges clearly.

points.title: Naming organic compounds (IUPAC)
points.content: 1. Find longest carbon chain = parent name. 2. Number from end nearest to substituents/functional groups. 3. Prefix substituents alphabetically with position numbers. 4. Suffix = principal functional group (ol, al, one, oic acid, amine, amide, ester). Ester: alkyl followed by parent acid -anoate.

points.title: Alkane reactions
points.content: Combustion: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O (complete). Free radical substitution: UV light required. Chain: initiation (Cl₂ → 2Cl•), propagation (Cl• + CH₄ → CH₃• + HCl; CH₃• + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•), termination (radical + radical → molecule).

points.title: Alkene reactions
points.content: Electrophilic addition: H₂ (Ni catalyst, hydrogenation), HX (Markovnikov), H₂O (H₃PO₄, steam, hydration), X₂ (halogenation, test for C=C), KMnO₄/H⁺ (oxidation, test). Polymerisation. Mechanism: electrophile attacks π bond → carbocation → nucleophile attacks.

points.title: Test for alkenes
points.content: Add bromine water (orange-brown): alkenes decolourise immediately (room temperature, no UV). Alkanes do NOT decolourise bromine water at room temperature. KMnO₄: alkenes decolourise purple → colourless (or brown MnO₂ in neutral conditions).

points.title: Markovnikov's rule explained
points.content: In addition of HX to unsymmetrical alkene, H adds to carbon with more H atoms. Reason: more substituted carbocation (2° or 3°) is more stable than 1° (alkyl groups donate electron density, stabilising + charge). Major product from more stable intermediate.

points.title: Cracking
points.content: Thermal cracking: high T (>800°C), high P, long chain → shorter chains + alkenes (free radical mechanism). Catalytic cracking: zeolite catalyst, ~500°C, produces more branched alkanes (better octane rating for fuels). Steam cracking: produces ethene for plastics.

points.title: Petroleum fractionation
points.content: Crude oil separated by fractional distillation. Fractions by decreasing boiling point: bitumen > fuel oil > diesel > kerosene > petrol > refinery gas. More C atoms → higher bp (stronger VdW). Reforming converts straight-chain to branched-chain alkanes.

points.title: SN1 vs SN2 mechanisms
points.content: SN2: one step, bimolecular, inversion of configuration (Walden inversion), favoured by primary halogenoalkanes and strong nucleophiles. SN1: two steps (carbocation intermediate), unimolecular, racemisation, favoured by tertiary halogenoalkanes and polar solvents.

points.title: Nucleophilic substitution reactions
points.content: With NaOH(aq): → alcohol (OH⁻ nucleophile, warm). With KCN(alc): → nitrile (CN⁻ nucleophile, chain extended by 1C). With NH₃(alc, excess, sealed tube): → amine. With AgNO₃(aq): → silver halide precipitate (tests for halide after hydrolysis).

points.title: Elimination reaction
points.content: Halogenoalkane + hot concentrated KOH in ethanol → alkene + KX + H₂O. Favoured by: tertiary halogenoalkanes, hot conditions, concentrated base. Competes with substitution (aqueous NaOH favours substitution; alcoholic KOH favours elimination).

points.title: Rate of hydrolysis
points.content: Add aqueous AgNO₃ + ethanol (warm). Time for precipitate: C–I fastest (weakest bond), C–Br medium, C–Cl slowest. C–F does not hydrolyse (too strong). This shows bond strength, NOT electronegativity, determines rate.

points.title: Environmental impact of CFCs
points.content: CFCs (e.g. CCl₂F₂) are very stable. In stratosphere: UV → Cl• radicals. Chain reaction: Cl• + O₃ → ClO• + O₂; ClO• + O• → Cl• + O₂. One Cl• destroys thousands of O₃ molecules. Replacement: HCFCs (less persistent) and HFCs (no Cl atoms).

points.title: Reactions of alcohols
points.content: Combustion: complete burning. Oxidation: 1° → aldehyde (distil off) → carboxylic acid. 2° → ketone. 3° → no oxidation. Reagent: K₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄ (orange → green). Dehydration: Al₂O₃ catalyst (180°C) → alkene. Esterification: carboxylic acid + H₂SO₄ catalyst (reversible). Reaction with Na: releases H₂.

points.title: Esterification mechanism and conditions
points.content: RCOOH + R'OH ⇌ RCOOR' + H₂O. Acid catalyst (H₂SO₄ or H₃PO₄), warm. Equilibrium: excess alcohol or acid, remove water to improve yield. Reverse (hydrolysis): add water + acid catalyst (or NaOH for irreversible saponification).

points.title: Properties of carboxylic acids
points.content: Weak acids (partially dissociate). Stronger than carbonic acid → react with carbonates (CO₂ produced). H-bonding (dimer formation) → relatively high bp. React with: Na, NaOH, Na₂CO₃/NaHCO₃ (all give CO₂ with carbonates).

points.title: Distinguishing aldehydes from carboxylic acids
points.content: Both contain C=O. Carboxylic acid: reacts with Na₂CO₃ (effervescence). Aldehyde: does NOT react with Na₂CO₃; gives silver mirror with Tollens'; gives brick-red precipitate with Fehling's solution.

points.title: Biodiesel and fats
points.content: Vegetable oils/animal fats: triglycerides (esters of glycerol + 3 fatty acids). Transesterification with methanol (NaOH catalyst): → biodiesel (FAME: fatty acid methyl esters) + glycerol. Biodiesel: renewable, lower net CO₂ emissions.

points.title: Nucleophilic addition mechanism to carbonyl
points.content: Step 1: nucleophile (e.g. CN⁻, HCN) attacks the δ+ carbon of C=O. Step 2: protonation of O⁻ intermediate by H⁺ (or H₂O). Product: addition compound (alcohol). Example: RCHO + HCN → RCH(OH)CN (hydroxynitrile).

points.title: Reduction of carbonyls
points.content: Reagent: NaBH₄ (in water/ethanol) or LiAlH₄ (in dry ether). Aldehyde → primary alcohol. Ketone → secondary alcohol. Mechanism: H⁻ (hydride ion) is the nucleophile attacking C=O carbon. NaBH₄ is safer (less vigorous) than LiAlH₄.

points.title: Tests to distinguish aldehydes and ketones
points.content: Tollens' reagent [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺: aldehyde → silver mirror (Ag deposited); ketone → no reaction. Fehling's solution (Cu²⁺ in NaOH/tartrate): aldehyde → brick-red Cu₂O precipitate; ketone → no reaction. Both oxidise aldehyde (RCHO → RCOOH).

points.title: Iodoform reaction (triiodomethane test)
points.content: Reagent: I₂/NaOH. Positive result (pale yellow CHI₃ precipitate + antiseptic smell) with: methyl ketones (CH₃COR), ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH), ethanal (CH₃CHO). Tests for CH₃C=O or CH₃CHOH group.

points.title: Aldol condensation
points.content: Two carbonyl compounds (with α-H) react under dilute NaOH (cold) → β-hydroxy carbonyl (aldol). On heating: dehydration → α,β-unsaturated carbonyl. Important in forming C–C bonds.

points.title: Cyanohydrin formation and use
points.content: RCH=O + HCN → RCH(OH)CN (with KCN/H⁺ or NaCN). Creates new chiral centre → racemic mixture. Cyanohydrin can be hydrolysed to α-hydroxy acid or reduced to amino alcohol. Extends carbon chain by 1.

points.title: Born-Haber cycle construction
points.content: Steps: 1. ΔHf° (formation of ionic compound). 2. ΔHat° of metal. 3. ΔHat° of non-metal. 4. IE (ionisation energy of metal). 5. EA (electron affinity of non-metal). 6. Lattice energy (ΔHlat). By Hess's Law: ΔHf° = ΔHat°(M) + ΔHat°(X) + IE + EA + ΔHlat.

points.title: Factors affecting lattice energy
points.content: Magnitude of lattice energy increases with: smaller ionic radius (ions closer together → stronger attraction) and higher ionic charge (more Coulombic force). |ΔHlat| order: MgO > CaO > NaCl > KCl. Na⁺ < K⁺ radius → NaCl more exothermic.

points.title: Theoretical vs experimental lattice energy
points.content: For NaCl: theoretical (purely ionic) ≈ experimental. For AgCl: experimental ΔHlat more negative than theoretical → greater covalent character (Ag⁺ is polarising, Cl⁻ is polarisable). Discrepancy indicates partial covalent character.

points.title: Enthalpy of solution cycle
points.content: ΔHsol = −ΔHlat(lattice dissociation) + ΔHhyd(cation) + ΔHhyd(anion). If ΔHhyd overcomes ΔHlat → soluble (ΔHsol negative or small positive). NaCl: slightly endothermic (+3.9 kJ/mol) but entropy drives dissolution.

points.title: Hydration enthalpy trends
points.content: More exothermic (more negative) for: smaller ionic radius (ion-dipole interactions stronger), higher charge. Li⁺ > Na⁺ > K⁺. Mg²⁺ >> Na⁺. Anions: F⁻ >> I⁻ (smaller, higher charge density).

points.title: Definitions: lattice energy, atomisation, electron affinity
points.content: Lattice energy: ΔH when 1 mol ionic compound formed from gaseous ions under standard conditions, e.g. Ca²⁺(g) + 2F⁻(g) → CaF₂(s). Atomisation ΔH: ΔH when 1 mol gaseous atoms formed from element in standard state, e.g. Ca(s) → Ca(g). 1st Electron Affinity: ΔH when 1 electron added to each atom in 1 mol gaseous atoms, e.g. I(g) + e⁻ → I⁻(g). 2nd EA is always endothermic (negatively charged ions repel electrons).

points.title: Electron affinity trends in Groups 16 and 17
points.content: Down Groups 16 and 17, 1st electron affinity decreases (less negative) from Cl to I, S to Te. Reason: more electron shells → greater shielding → outer electrons further from nucleus → weaker attraction for added electron.

points.title: Effect of ionic charge and radius on lattice energy magnitude
points.content: Same cation, same anion charge: as ionic radius increases (e.g. F⁻ → I⁻), lattice enthalpy becomes less exothermic (e.g. NaF > NaCl > NaBr > NaI). Doubly charged ions (Mg²⁺O²⁻, ΔHlat = −3923 kJ/mol) give much more exothermic lattice energy than singly charged (Li⁺F⁻, ΔHlat = −1050 kJ/mol).

points.title: ΔHsol = −ΔHlat + ΣΔHhyd equation
points.content: ΔHsol(MgCl₂) = −ΔHlat(MgCl₂) + ΔHhyd(Mg²⁺) + 2ΔHhyd(Cl⁻). Hydration enthalpies become less exothermic down Group II as ionic radius increases → charge density decreases → weaker ion-dipole attraction with water.

points.title: Polarising power and thermal stability trends
points.content: Polarising power of cation: ability to attract electrons and distort anion. Down Group II: M²⁺ radius increases → charge density decreases → polarising power decreases → less distortion of CO₃²⁻/NO₃⁻ electron cloud → thermal stability of carbonates and nitrates INCREASES down the group.

points.title: Solubility trends of Group II sulfates and hydroxides
points.content: Sulfate solubility DECREASES down group: as M²⁺ radius increases, both lattice enthalpy and hydration enthalpy decrease, but change in lattice enthalpy is smaller (large SO₄²⁻ dominates) → ΔHsol becomes less exothermic/more endothermic. Hydroxide solubility INCREASES down group: small OH⁻ means ΔHhyd change dominates over ΔHlat change → ΔHsol more exothermic.

points.title: Standard electrode potential measurement
points.content: Requires: standard hydrogen electrode (SHE, E° = 0.00 V) as reference. Standard conditions: 298 K, 1 mol dm⁻³ ion concentration, 100 kPa for gases. Connect with salt bridge (KNO₃) to complete circuit.

points.title: Predicting cell EMF and spontaneity
points.content: E°cell = E°(cathode) − E°(anode) = E°(more +ve) − E°(less +ve). If E°cell > 0: reaction is spontaneous (feasible). The species with more positive E° is reduced (is the oxidising agent). Reaction at anode: oxidation. Cathode: reduction.

points.title: Limitations of E° predictions
points.content: E° values predict thermodynamic feasibility only. Kinetic barriers (high Ea) may prevent reaction. Conditions (non-standard T, concentration) affect actual potentials (Nernst equation). A reaction may be feasible but imperceptibly slow.

points.title: Electrolysis: predicting products
points.content: At cathode (−): cation with most positive (least negative) E° is discharged. At anode (+): anion with most negative E° is discharged. In practice: overpotential means Cl⁻ discharged preferentially over OH⁻ in concentrated NaCl(aq). At inert anode: O₂ from dilute solutions, Cl₂ from concentrated Cl⁻.

points.title: Faraday's laws calculations
points.content: Q = It (charge = current × time). Moles of electrons = Q/F (F = 96485 C mol⁻¹ ≈ 96500). Moles of product = moles electrons / number of electrons in half-equation. Mass = moles × molar mass.

points.title: Fuel cells
points.content: H₂-O₂ fuel cell: H₂ + ½O₂ → H₂O. Anode: H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻. Cathode: ½O₂ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂O. Advantages: higher efficiency than combustion engine, only water produced. Disadvantages: H₂ storage, expensive catalysts (Pt).

points.title: Standard hydrogen electrode (SHE) construction
points.content: H₂ gas at 1 atm bubbled through 1.0 mol dm⁻³ H⁺(aq) using platinum electrode (coated with Pt black). Half-equation: 2H⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ H₂(g), E° = 0.00 V. Used as reference to measure E° of any half-cell connected via salt bridge and voltmeter at 298 K.

points.title: Cell diagrams for different half-cell types
points.content: Metal/cation (e.g. Cr³⁺/Cr): Cr rod in Cr³⁺ solution, connected to SHE via salt bridge. Non-metal/anion (e.g. Cl₂/Cl⁻): Pt electrode in Cl⁻ solution with Cl₂ gas at 1 atm. Same element different oxidation states (e.g. MnO₄⁻/Mn²⁺): Pt electrode in solution containing both ions with H⁺.

points.title: Nernst equation applications with worked examples
points.content: E = E° + (0.059/z) × log([oxidised]/[reduced]) at 298 K. Example: MnO₂ + 4HCl → MnCl₂ + Cl₂ + 2H₂O — not feasible under standard conditions (ΔE = −0.13 V), but using concentrated HCl increases [H⁺] (raises E of MnO₂/Mn²⁺) and increases [Cl⁻] (lowers E of Cl₂/Cl⁻), making Ecell positive → reaction occurs.

points.title: Electrolysis product prediction using electrode potentials
points.content: At cathode (−): species with more positive E° is reduced. In aqueous solution, metal ions compete with 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ (E°=0.0 V). At anode (+): species with more negative E° is oxidised. Non-metal anions compete with 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻. High [Cl⁻] → Cl₂ produced; dilute [Cl⁻] → O₂ produced.

points.title: Determining Avogadro constant by electrolysis
points.content: Electrolyse CuSO₄(aq) with Cu electrodes. Measure: current I, time t, mass change of anode (more accurate than cathode — deposited Cu may detach). Calculate: Q = I×t, n(Cu) = m(Cu)/63.5, n(e⁻) = n(Cu)×2, F = Q/n(e⁻), L = F/(1.60×10⁻¹⁹).

points.title: ΔG° = −nFE°cell relationship
points.content: ΔG° = −nFE°cell. For voltaic/galvanic cells: E°cell > 0 → ΔG° < 0 → spontaneous, electrical energy produced. For electrolytic cells: E°cell < 0 → ΔG° > 0 → non-spontaneous, electrical energy must be supplied to force reaction.

points.title: pH calculations
points.content: Strong acid: [H⁺] = c(acid) → pH = −log(c). Strong base: [OH⁻] = c(base), pOH = −log[OH⁻], pH = 14 − pOH. Weak acid: [H⁺] = √(Ka × c) assuming Ka << c. Buffer: [H⁺] = Ka × [HA]/[A⁻], pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]).

points.title: Buffer action explained
points.content: Buffer = weak acid HA + its salt (A⁻). Add H⁺: HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻ shifts left (H⁺ + A⁻ → HA). Add OH⁻: HA + OH⁻ → A⁻ + H₂O (weak acid neutralises OH⁻). pH ≈ pKa when [HA] = [A⁻] (half-equivalence point).

points.title: Indicators and titration curves
points.content: Indicator works at pH = pKIn ± 1. Choose indicator whose pKIn falls in the vertical part of the titration curve. Strong acid–strong base: any indicator (phenolphthalein or methyl orange). Weak acid–strong base: phenolphthalein. Strong acid–weak base: methyl orange. Weak acid–weak base: no sharp endpoint.

points.title: Hydrolysis of salts
points.content: NH₄Cl: NH₄⁺ + H₂O ⇌ NH₃ + H₃O⁺ → acidic. Na₂CO₃: CO₃²⁻ + H₂O ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + OH⁻ → alkaline. NaCl: no hydrolysis → neutral. Al(NO₃)₃: Al³⁺ hydrolyses → acidic.

points.title: Kw and its temperature dependence
points.content: Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 10⁻¹⁴ at 298 K. pH of pure water = 7 at 298 K. As T increases, Kw increases (ionisation of water is endothermic). At 50°C, Kw > 10⁻¹⁴ → pH < 7, but water is still neutral ([H⁺] = [OH⁻]).

points.title: Solubility product (Ksp)
points.content: For MₐNb ⇌ aM^(b+) + bN^(a-): Ksp = [M^(b+)]^a × [N^(a-)]^b. If ionic product > Ksp: precipitate forms. Solubility s relates to Ksp. Common ion effect: adding a common ion decreases solubility (drives equilibrium back).

points.title: Conjugate acid-base pairs
points.content: Conjugate acid-base pairs: two species that differ by one proton (H⁺). Acid donates proton; base accepts proton. An acid can be neutral molecule, positive ion, or negative ion. The weaker the acid, the stronger its conjugate base. Examples: CH₃COOH/CH₃COO⁻, NH₄⁺/NH₃, H₂O/OH⁻.

points.title: Ka and pKa calculation methods
points.content: For weak acid HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻: Ka = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA], pKa = −log Ka. Method 1 (known c, Ka): [H⁺] = √(Ka×c), pH = −log[H⁺]. Method 2 (known c, measured pH): [H⁺] = 10^(−pH), Ka = [H⁺]²/(c−[H⁺]) ≈ [H⁺]²/c. Larger Ka = stronger acid; smaller pKa = stronger acid.

points.title: Four types of buffer systems with ionic equations
points.content: (1) CH₃COOH/CH₃COONa (pKa~4.7): add H⁺ → CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺ → CH₃COOH; add OH⁻ → CH₃COOH + OH⁻ → CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O. (2) NH₃/NH₄Cl (pKa~9.25): add H⁺ → NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺; add OH⁻ → NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃ + H₂O. (3) NaH₂PO₄/Na₂HPO₄ (pKa~7.2). (4) NaHCO₃/Na₂CO₃ (pKa~10.2). HCO₃⁻ in blood controls pH.

points.title: Buffer calculation methods — three types
points.content: Type 1: Given [HA], [A⁻] and pKa: [H⁺] = Ka×[HA]/[A⁻], pH = pKa − log([HA]/[A⁻]). Type 2: Find [HA]/[A⁻] ratio for target pH: [HA]/[A⁻] = 10^(pKa−pH). Type 3: Mix weak acid with NaOH — calculate [HA] and [A⁻] after neutralisation, then apply Henderson-Hasselbalch. At half-equivalence point: pH = pKa.

points.title: Common ion effect and Ksp calculations
points.content: Common ion effect: solubility of a sparingly soluble salt DECREASES when dissolved in a solution containing a common ion (Le Chatelier). Example: solubility of AgBr in 5.8×10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ AgNO₃: [Br⁻] = Ksp/[Ag⁺] = 7.7×10⁻¹³/5.8×10⁻³. If ionic product Qsp > Ksp, precipitate forms.

points.title: Partition coefficient Kpc definition and calculations
points.content: Kpc = [X(solvent B)]/[X(solvent A)] at equilibrium at a particular temperature. 'Like dissolves like' — Kpc depends on relative solubilities and strength of intermolecular bonds. Example: Ammonia Kpc (water/CHCl₃) > 1 because NH₃ forms H-bonds with water but only dipole-dipole with CHCl₃. Iodine Kpc (organic/water) > 1 because I₂ and organic solvents are nonpolar.

points.title: Determining rate equation from initial rates
points.content: Compare experiments keeping all concentrations constant except one. If doubling [A] doubles rate → 1st order in A. If doubling [A] quadruples rate → 2nd order. If no change → 0th order. Repeat for each reactant. Then calculate k from rate = k[A]^m[B]^n.

points.title: Graphical methods for order
points.content: 0th order: [A] vs t = straight line with negative gradient (gradient = −k). 1st order: ln[A] vs t = straight line (gradient = −k), constant t½. 2nd order: 1/[A] vs t = straight line (gradient = k).

points.title: Arrhenius equation and graph
points.content: k = A·e^(−Ea/RT). Taking ln: ln k = ln A − Ea/RT. Plot ln k vs 1/T: gradient = −Ea/R → Ea = −gradient × R. Intercept = ln A. As T increases, k increases (exponential relationship).

points.title: Deducing mechanism from rate equation
points.content: Rate equation indicates which species are involved in the rate-determining step (RDS) and their molecularity. Only species in the rate equation appear in the RDS. Example: rate = k[A][B²] → A and 2 molecules of B in RDS. Propose mechanism consistent with overall equation and rate law.

points.title: Catalysis and rate
points.content: Catalyst provides alternative pathway with lower Ea. Does NOT change ΔH or equilibrium position (for reversible reactions). Heterogeneous: different phase (Fe in Haber, Pt in catalytic converter). Homogeneous: same phase (H⁺ in esterification, Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺ in S₂O₈²⁻ + I⁻ reaction).

points.title: Half-life method for determining reaction order
points.content: Zero order: half-life DECREASES as concentration decreases (t½ = [A]₀/2k). First order: half-life is CONSTANT regardless of concentration (t½ = ln2/k); after n half-lives, [A] = [A]₀/2ⁿ. Second order: half-life INCREASES/DOUBLES as concentration decreases (t½ = 1/k[A]₀). Identify from [A] vs time graph shape.

points.title: Rate equations for SN1 and SN2 mechanisms
points.content: SN2 (bimolecular, primary halogenoalkane): single-step — nucleophile attacks from back, transition state, product. Rate = k[RX][Nu⁻], second order overall. SN1 (unimolecular, tertiary halogenoalkane): two-step — slow loss of halide → carbocation intermediate, then fast nucleophile attack. Rate = k[RX], first order overall.

points.title: Mechanism deduction: matching rate equation to steps
points.content: Only species in the rate equation (with correct orders) appear in the slowest/rate-determining step. Example: 2NO + Br₂ → 2NOBr, Rate = k[NO][Br₂] → slow step must involve 1 NO + 1 Br₂ (Mechanism B). Species NOT in rate equation appear in fast steps after RDS.

points.title: Rate constant relationship with temperature and Ea
points.content: Rate constant k increases as T increases (Arrhenius: k = Ae^(−Ea/RT)). k decreases as Ea increases. The activation energy and temperature do NOT appear in the rate equation itself, but affect k.

points.title: Surface catalysis: adsorption, reaction, desorption
points.content: Heterogeneous catalysis mechanism: (1) Adsorption — reactants bond to catalyst surface, bonds weaken. (2) Reaction — weakened bonds react on surface, Ea lowered. (3) Desorption — products leave surface. Example: Fe in Haber Process, Ni in ethene hydrogenation.

points.title: Three-way catalytic converter
points.content: Catalyst: Pt/Pd/Rh. Converts toxic exhaust: 2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂; 4CO + 2NO₂ → 4CO₂ + N₂; 2CO + O₂ → 2CO₂. Transition metals are good catalysts because: variable oxidation states (transfer electrons), vacant d orbitals that are energetically accessible (form coordinate bonds to weaken bonds in reactants).

points.title: Entropy changes
points.content: S increases when: solid → liquid → gas; dissolving; mixing; number of gas moles increases; temperature increases. S decreases when: gases condense; precipitation; number of gas moles decreases. ΔSsystem = ΣS(products) − ΣS(reactants).

points.title: Total entropy and spontaneity
points.content: ΔStotal = ΔSsystem + ΔSsurroundings. ΔSsurroundings = −ΔH/T. A process is spontaneous when ΔStotal > 0. This is equivalent to ΔG < 0 (since ΔG = −TΔStotal).

points.title: ΔG analysis for different conditions
points.content: ΔH < 0, ΔS > 0: always spontaneous (ΔG always negative). ΔH > 0, ΔS < 0: never spontaneous. ΔH < 0, ΔS < 0: spontaneous at low T (when |TΔS| < |ΔH|). ΔH > 0, ΔS > 0: spontaneous at high T (when TΔS > ΔH). Feasibility temperature: T = ΔH/ΔS.

points.title: ΔG and equilibrium constant
points.content: ΔG° = −RT ln K. If K > 1: ΔG° < 0 (products favoured). If K < 1: ΔG° > 0 (reactants favoured). If K = 1: ΔG° = 0. At equilibrium: ΔG = 0 (not ΔG°). Standard value vs actual value: ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q.

points.title: Electrochemistry link to ΔG
points.content: ΔG° = −nFE°cell. Where n = moles of electrons transferred, F = Faraday constant (96500 C mol⁻¹). If E°cell > 0: ΔG° < 0 (spontaneous). Consistent with K: ΔG° = −RT ln K = −nFE°.

points.title: Predicting sign of entropy change ΔS
points.content: ΔS > 0 (positive) when: solid → liquid → gas; dissolving; number of gas molecules increases; temperature increases. ΔS < 0 (negative) when: gas → liquid → solid; precipitation; number of gas molecules decreases. ΔS° = ΣS°(products) − ΣS°(reactants).

points.title: Calculating transfer/crossover temperature
points.content: At the temperature where reaction becomes feasible: ΔG = 0 = ΔH − TΔS, so T = ΔH/ΔS. Assume ΔH and ΔS are constant with temperature. Example: Fe₂O₃(s) + 3H₂(g) → 2Fe(s) + 3H₂O(g), T > 696 K for spontaneity.

points.title: Feasibility conditions summary table
points.content: ΔH < 0, ΔS > 0: always feasible (ΔG always negative). ΔH > 0, ΔS < 0: never feasible (ΔG always positive). ΔH < 0, ΔS < 0: feasible at low T (when |ΔH| > |TΔS|). ΔH > 0, ΔS > 0: feasible at high T (when |TΔS| > |ΔH|). At equilibrium: ΔG = 0.

points.title: Calculating ΔG° from standard free energies of formation
points.content: ΔG° = ΣΔG°f(products) − ΣΔG°f(reactants). Example: combustion of ethanol C₂H₅OH(l) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(g). ΔG° = 2(−394.4) + 3(−228.6) − (−174.8) − 3(0) = −1299.6 kJ mol⁻¹.

points.title: Definition and properties of transition elements
points.content: d-block elements that form at least one stable ion with incomplete d sub-shell (Ti to Cu; Sc and Zn excluded). Properties: variable oxidation states, coloured ions, catalytic activity, complex ion formation, paramagnetic.

points.title: Electronic configurations
points.content: General: [Ar] 3d^n 4s². Exceptions: Cr = [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹; Cu = [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ (extra stability of half-full and full d shells). When forming ions: 4s electrons lost first, then 3d. Fe³⁺ = [Ar] 3d⁵ (half-full d, stable).

points.title: Colour of complex ions
points.content: Due to d-d transition: ligands cause d orbital splitting (crystal field splitting). Electron absorbs visible light, moves from lower to higher d orbital. Complementary colour is observed. More splitting → shorter wavelength absorbed → different colour. [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ blue; [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺ deep blue; [Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺ pale violet.

points.title: Common complex ions
points.content: [Fe(H₂O)₆]²⁺: green. [Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺: pale violet/brown. [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺: light blue. [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺: deep blue. [Cr(H₂O)₆]³⁺: green-violet. [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺: pink. [Fe(SCN)(H₂O)₅]²⁺: blood red (test for Fe³⁺). [FeCl₄]⁻: yellow.

points.title: Ligand substitution reactions
points.content: H₂O replaced by stronger ligands. Cu²⁺(aq) + 4NH₃ → [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺ + 4H₂O (deepen blue; add excess NH₃ to Cu(OH)₂ precipitate). Fe³⁺(aq) + SCN⁻ → [Fe(SCN)]²⁺ (blood red; test for Fe³⁺). Haemoglobin: Fe²⁺ centre, O₂ ligand; CO binds more strongly → poisoning.

points.title: Redox reactions of vanadium
points.content: V can exist as +5, +4, +3, +2. Reduction by Zn in acidic solution: VO₂⁺ (yellow, +5) → VO²⁺ (blue, +4) → V³⁺ (green, +3) → V²⁺ (violet, +2). This demonstrates variable oxidation states of transition metals.

points.title: Stability constant (Kstab)
points.content: For [ML_n]^(a+) ⇌ M^(a+) + nL. Kstab = [M^(a+)][L]^n / [[ML_n]^(a+)] ... actually Kstab = product/reactants for formation. Large Kstab → stable complex. EDTA⁴⁻ forms very stable complexes with 4-coordinate binding (chelation); used in medicine (treatment of metal poisoning).

points.title: Why Sc and Zn are NOT transition elements
points.content: Sc forms only one ion Sc³⁺ [Ar]3d⁰ (3d empty). Zn forms only one ion Zn²⁺ [Ar]3d¹⁰ (3d full). Neither forms a stable ion with incomplete d sub-shell. This is the defining criterion for transition elements.

points.title: Explanation of variable oxidation states
points.content: Due to the similarity in energy of 3d and 4s sub-shells, both 4s and 3d electrons can be involved in bonding. Lower oxidation states: found in ionic compounds. Higher oxidation states: found in compounds with O or F (e.g. VO₂⁺, Cr₂O₇²⁻, MnO₄⁻).

points.title: Types of ligands: monodentate, bidentate, polydentate
points.content: Monodentate: donate 1 lone pair (H₂O:, :NH₃, Cl⁻, CN⁻, SCN⁻). Bidentate: donate 2 lone pairs (H₂NCH₂CH₂NH₂ 'en', C₂O₄²⁻ ethanedioate). Polydentate: hexadentate EDTA⁴⁻ donates 6 lone pairs — forms very stable complexes (chelation effect).

points.title: Complex geometries by coordination number
points.content: Coordination 2: linear, [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺, bond angle 180°. Coordination 4: tetrahedral [CuCl₄]²⁻ (109.5°) OR square planar [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻ (90°). Coordination 6: octahedral [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺, [Cr(H₂O)₄Cl₂]⁺, bond angle 90°. Shape determined by ligand type and metal ion.

points.title: Ligand substitution of Cu(II) — complete reaction scheme
points.content: [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ (blue) + 2OH⁻ → Cu(OH)₂(H₂O)₄↓ (pale blue ppt). + 2NH₃ → same ppt. + excess NH₃ → [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺ (deep blue). + conc HCl → [CuCl₄]²⁻ (yellow-green, tetrahedral). + excess NH₃ → back to deep blue [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺. Kstab: [CuCl₄]²⁻ ≈ 10⁵, [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ ≈ 10¹².

points.title: Ligand substitution of Co(II) — colour changes
points.content: [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺ (pink) + OH⁻ → Co(OH)₂(H₂O)₄↓ (blue ppt) → warmed → brown ppt. + NH₃ → blue ppt → excess NH₃ → [Co(NH₃)₆]²⁺ (brown solution). + conc HCl → [CoCl₄]²⁻ (blue solution). Anhydrous CoCl₂ paper: blue → pink with water (test for water).

points.title: d-orbital splitting in octahedral and tetrahedral complexes
points.content: In octahedral: ligands approach along x, y, z axes → degenerate d orbitals split into two sets: lower energy t₂g (dxy, dxz, dyz) and higher energy eg (dx²−y², dz²). In tetrahedral: splitting is REVERSED — eg orbitals are LOWER energy than t₂. ΔE (crystal field splitting energy) determines colour: electron absorbs visible light → d-d transition → complementary colour transmitted.

points.title: Stereoisomerism in transition metal complexes
points.content: Cis-trans isomerism: in square planar complexes (e.g. cis-platin vs trans-platin) and octahedral [MA₄B₂] (cis: B ligands at 90°; trans: B ligands at 180°). Optical isomerism: occurs with 2 or 3 bidentate ligands in octahedral complexes — non-superimposable mirror images. Three bidentate ligands (e.g. [Ni(en)₃]²⁺) always give optical isomers.

points.title: Evidence for benzene structure
points.content: Kekulé's alternating double bonds predicts: two forms of 1,2-disubstituted benzene (not observed), high reactivity to Br₂ (not seen), ΔHhyd more negative than expected. Actual evidence: all C-C bonds equal length (139 pm), thermodynamic stability (ΔHhyd less negative by ~150 kJ/mol = delocalisation energy), no addition reactions with bromine water.

points.title: Electrophilic substitution mechanism
points.content: General: Ar–H + E⁺ → [Ar–H–E]⁺ (arenium ion/σ-complex) → Ar–E + H⁺. The ring is restored (aromaticity retained) by loss of H⁺. Nitration: E⁺ = NO₂⁺ (from HNO₃ + H₂SO₄). Halogenation: E⁺ from X₂ + AlX₃ (Lewis acid catalyst).

points.title: Nitration conditions and mechanism
points.content: Conc. HNO₃ + conc. H₂SO₄, 50-55°C (not higher: polynitration). Generation of NO₂⁺: HNO₃ + H₂SO₄ → NO₂⁺ + HSO₄⁻ + H₂O. NO₂⁺ attacks ring → σ-complex → lose H⁺ to HSO₄⁻ → nitrobenzene.

points.title: Friedel-Crafts reactions
points.content: Alkylation: ArH + RCl + AlCl₃ → Ar–R + HCl + AlCl₃. Acylation: ArH + RCOCl + AlCl₃ → Ar–COR + HCl + AlCl₃. AlCl₃ is Lewis acid catalyst: generates R⁺ or RCO⁺ (acylium). Acylation preferred in synthesis (no rearrangement, product deactivated → monosubstitution only).

points.title: Directing effects of substituents
points.content: Activating (2,4-directors): –OH, –NH₂, –OCH₃ (donate electrons into ring by resonance). Deactivating (3-directors): –NO₂, –CN, –COOH, –CHO (withdraw electrons). Halogens: deactivating but 2,4-directors (lone pairs donate but electronegative). Use directing effects to plan synthesis routes.

points.title: Reactions of phenol
points.content: Phenol is more reactive than benzene (–OH activates ring). Reacts with Br₂(aq) without catalyst → 2,4,6-tribromophenol (white precipitate, test for phenol). Reacts with NaOH → sodium phenoxide (phenol is weakly acidic, pKa ~10). Does NOT react with Na₂CO₃.

points.title: Benzene bonding and shape description
points.content: Each C is sp² hybridised, forming two C–C σ-bonds (sp²–sp²) and one C–H σ-bond (sp²–s). Trigonal planar geometry around each C, bond angles 120°, hexagonal planar molecule. Unhybridised 2p orbitals overlap to form delocalised π-system above and below the ring. All C–C bonds equal length (139 pm), intermediate between C–C and C=C.

points.title: Directing effects: 2,4-directing vs 3,5-directing explanation
points.content: 2,4-directing (activating) groups — –R/alkyl, –OH, –NH₂: alkyl groups donate electrons inductively; –OH and –NH₂ have lone pairs delocalised into π-system → increases electron density at 2,4,6-positions → more readily attracts electrophile. 3,5-directing (deactivating) groups — –NO₂, –CO₂H, –COR: withdraw electrons from ring → reduce electron density → less readily attracts electrophile.

points.title: Relative acidities: water, ethanol, phenol
points.content: Acidity order: CH₃CH₂OH < H₂O < phenol. Ethanol: alkyl group donates electrons → strengthens O–H bond. Phenol: lone pair on O delocalised into benzene ring → weakens O–H bond; phenoxide ion is stabilised by delocalisation (negative charge spread over the whole ion). pKa: ethanol > water (≈15.7) > phenol (≈10).

points.title: Acidity of carboxylic acids vs alcohols explained
points.content: Carboxylic acids are much stronger acids than alcohols. Two explanations: (1) C=O group withdraws electrons from O–H, weakening the bond. OR (2) Carboxylate anion R–COO⁻ is stabilised by delocalisation — negative charge spread over the whole –CO₂⁻ group, both C–O bonds equal length. pKa: carboxylic acids ≈ 4–5 vs alcohols ≈ 15–18.

points.title: Acidity of chlorine-substituted carboxylic acids
points.content: As more Cl atoms replace H in methyl group, acidity INCREASES: CH₃COOH (pKa=4.74) < CH₂ClCOOH (2.86) < CHCl₂COOH (1.26) < CCl₃COOH (0.64). Electronegative Cl atoms withdraw electrons from –CO₂H group, weakening O–H bond AND stabilising carboxylate anion. Alkyl groups have opposite (electron-donating) effect: HCOOH > CH₃COOH > CH₃CH₂COOH.

points.title: Relative ease of hydrolysis: acyl > alkyl > aryl chlorides
points.content: Acyl chlorides: hydrolysis at room temperature by addition-elimination. O and Cl both electron-withdrawing → C=O carbon carries more δ+ → more readily attacked. Alkyl chlorides: need heat under reflux, nucleophilic substitution. Alkyl group donates electrons → C–Cl bond stronger. Aryl chlorides: no reaction even boiled with NaOH. p-orbital of Cl overlaps with delocalised π-system → C–Cl has partial double bond character → strengthened.

points.title: Reactivity order
points.content: Acyl chloride > acid anhydride > carboxylic acid > ester > amide. Decreasing reactivity towards nucleophiles (better leaving groups make more reactive). Acyl chlorides react violently with water; amides hydrolyse slowly.

points.title: Reactions of acyl chlorides
points.content: With water: RCOC1 + H₂O → RCOOH + HCl (vigorous, fumes). With alcohol: RCOCl + R'OH → RCOOR' + HCl (ester, no catalyst, room temperature). With amine: RCOCl + R'NH₂ → RCONHR' + HCl (amide). With ammonia: RCOCl + NH₃ → RCONH₂ + HCl.

points.title: Reactions of acid anhydrides
points.content: Similar to acyl chlorides but less vigorous. With water: (RCO)₂O + H₂O → 2RCOOH. With alcohol: → ester + carboxylic acid (not ester + HCl). With amine: → amide + carboxylic acid. Ethanoic anhydride used industrially (safer, no HCl evolved).

points.title: Mechanism: addition-elimination
points.content: Step 1: nucleophile (e.g. OH⁻ or H₂O) adds to C=O → tetrahedral intermediate. Step 2: leaving group (Cl⁻ from acyl chloride, RCOO⁻ from anhydride) is expelled, C=O restored. Net result: substitution at carbonyl carbon.

points.title: Hydrolysis of esters
points.content: Acid hydrolysis (H₂SO₄/H₂O, heat): reversible, gives carboxylic acid + alcohol. Alkaline hydrolysis / saponification (NaOH/H₂O, heat): irreversible, gives carboxylate salt + alcohol (used in soap making). Alkaline faster and complete.

points.title: Basicity of amines
points.content: Amines are bases: lone pair on N accepts H⁺. pKb: alkyl amines (~3-4, stronger than NH₃) < NH₃ (~4.7) < aryl amines (~9). Phenylamine weaker base: lone pair delocalised into benzene ring. Alkyl groups donate electrons → increase lone pair availability.

points.title: Reactions of amines
points.content: With acids: RNH₂ + HCl → RNH₃⁺Cl⁻ (salt). With acyl chlorides: → amide + HCl. As nucleophile (nucleophilic substitution): attack halogenoalkane → secondary amine (then tertiary, then quaternary ammonium). With nitrous acid: ArNH₂ + HNO₂ → ArN₂⁺ (diazonium salt, 0-5°C).

points.title: Amino acids properties
points.content: Zwitterion: –NH₃⁺ and –COO⁻ simultaneously. Isoelectric point (pI): pH at which molecule carries no net charge; amine and carboxyl groups both in ionic form. In acidic solution: –NH₃⁺ group predominates (cation). In alkaline: –COO⁻ group (anion). Forms peptides via condensation.

points.title: Diazonium salt reactions
points.content: Formed: ArNH₂ + NaNO₂ + HCl, 0-5°C → ArN₂⁺Cl⁻. Must keep cold (decomposes above 5°C). Coupling with phenol (alkaline): ArN₂⁺ + ArOH → Ar-N=N-Ar' (azo dye, orange-yellow). Coupling with aryl amines (weakly acidic): → red/orange azo compound.

points.title: Polyamides (nylon)
points.content: Nylon-6,6: hexan-1,6-diamine + hexanedioic acid → [-NH-(CH₂)₆-NH-CO-(CH₂)₄-CO-]n + H₂O. Amide bonds between each monomer unit. H-bonds between chains → strong, tough fibre. Peptide bonds in proteins also amide bonds.

points.title: Amino acids: zwitterion and isoelectric point
points.content: Amino acids exist as zwitterions (H₃N⁺–CHR–COO⁻) in solid state and neutral aqueous solution. In acid: –COO⁻ accepts H⁺ → cationic form H₃N⁺–CHR–COOH. In base: –NH₃⁺ donates H⁺ → anionic form H₂N–CHR–COO⁻. Isoelectric point (pI): the pH at which the amino acid carries zero net charge. At pI, amino acid does NOT migrate in electrophoresis.

points.title: Peptide bond formation
points.content: Two amino acids condense: carboxylic acid group of one reacts with amino group of another → amide/peptide bond (–CONH–) + H₂O. Dipeptide → tripeptide → polypeptide. Backbone has N–C–C repeating pattern. N-terminus (free –NH₂ end) and C-terminus (free –COOH end). Side chains (R groups) determine properties.

points.title: Basicity comparison: amines, ammonia, phenylamine, amide
points.content: Basicity order: 3° amine > 2° amine > 1° amine > NH₃ > phenylamine > amide. Amines: alkyl groups donate electrons → lone pair on N more available. Phenylamine: lone pair delocalised into benzene ring → less available. Amide: lone pair delocalised by electron-withdrawing C=O → least available. Amines react with HCl → RNH₃⁺Cl⁻; amides do NOT react with HCl.

points.title: Addition polymers
points.content: Monomer contains C=C double bond. Opens to form long chain; no other product. Examples: poly(ethene) from ethene, PVC from chloroethene, PTFE from tetrafluoroethene. Repeat unit loses one C=C: –[CH₂–CHX]n–. Problems: non-biodegradable, difficult to recycle.

points.title: Condensation polymers
points.content: Two functional groups react, losing small molecule (H₂O or HCl) each time. Polyesters: diol + dicarboxylic acid → –[O–R–O–CO–R'–CO]n– + H₂O. Polyamides: diamine + diacid (or diacyl chloride) → –[NH–R–NH–CO–R'–CO]n– + H₂O (or HCl).

points.title: Drawing repeat units
points.content: Addition: draw the repeat unit from monomer (remove the double bond, put single bond between units). Condensation: identify the bonds formed between monomers (ester –COO– or amide –CONH–); show the atoms lost. Include brackets with n.

points.title: Hydrolysis of condensation polymers
points.content: Polyesters hydrolyse in acid or alkali (break ester bonds → diol + diacid/salt). Polyamides hydrolyse in acid or alkali (break amide bonds → diamine + diacid). Addition polymers (C–C backbone) do NOT hydrolyse. This is why polyesters/polyamides are biodegradable.

points.title: Kevlar and other engineering polymers
points.content: Kevlar: polyamide from benzene-1,4-diamine + benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid. Highly ordered H-bonds between parallel chains → exceptional strength. Used in body armour, tyres. Terylene (PET): polyester from ethylene glycol + terephthalic acid; used in fibres, bottles.

points.title: Polyesters from hydroxycarboxylic acids (PLA example)
points.content: Poly(lactic acid) PLA: formed from lactic acid HO–CH(CH₃)–COOH monomers. Each monomer has both –OH and –COOH → condensation polymerisation without needing two different monomers. PLA is biodegradable and used in medical implants and compostable packaging.

points.title: Polyamides from amino acids (polypeptide)
points.content: Amino acids can polymerise via peptide bonds to form polypeptides/proteins. Each amino acid has –NH₂ and –COOH groups → self-condensation. Repeat unit contains N–C–C backbone with amide (–CONH–) linkage.

points.title: Photodegradable and biodegradable polymers
points.content: Poly(alkenes) are chemically inert → difficult to biodegrade. Polyesters and polyamides contain C=O (carbonyl) groups that absorb UV light → bonds weaken and break down (photodegradable). Both are also biodegradable: acid or alkaline hydrolysis breaks ester/amide linkages back to monomers. This is why condensation polymers are more environmentally friendly than addition polymers.

points.title: Key functional group interconversions
points.content: Alkene → alkane (H₂/Ni), → alcohol (H₂O/acid), → halogenoalkane (HX), → diol (cold KMnO₄). Halogenoalkane → alcohol (NaOH/H₂O), → nitrile (KCN/alc), → amine (NH₃/alc), → alkene (KOH/alc, hot). Primary alcohol → aldehyde → carboxylic acid. Secondary alcohol → ketone. Aldehyde → primary alcohol (NaBH₄).

points.title: Carbon chain extension methods
points.content: +1C: Nucleophilic substitution with KCN/HCN (nitrile) → then hydrolysis to carboxylic acid. +1C: via Grignard reagent (A-level context: RMgX + CO₂ → carboxylic acid). Friedel-Crafts acylation extends chain on benzene ring.

points.title: Planning a synthesis route
points.content: 1. Identify carbon skeleton changes needed. 2. Identify functional group at start vs end. 3. Work backwards (retrosynthesis): what reaction produces target from simpler molecule? 4. Check reagents and conditions are known. 5. Consider stereochemistry (chiral products, geometric isomers).

points.title: Controlling reaction type
points.content: Halogenoalkane: with NaOH(aq) → substitution (alcohol). With KOH in ethanol → elimination (alkene). With NH₃(excess) → amine. With KCN → nitrile. Alcohol: oxidation conditions determine aldehyde vs carboxylic acid.

points.title: Protection of functional groups
points.content: When a reaction would attack a sensitive group, protect it first. Example: to reduce ester without reducing acid: convert acid to ester temporarily. In peptide synthesis: protect –NH₂ as N-Boc amine, then deprotect. A-level: understand the principle of using protecting groups.

points.title: Optical activity and racemic mixtures in synthesis
points.content: Optically active substance rotates plane-polarised light. Two enantiomers rotate by equal amounts in opposite directions. Racemic mixture (racemate): 50:50 mixture of both enantiomers → optically inactive (no net rotation). In drug design, using a pure single enantiomer: reduces dosage by half, better therapeutic activity, minimises risk of side effects from the unwanted enantiomer.

points.title: Mass spectrometry interpretation
points.content: Molecular ion (M⁺): highest m/z peak (excluding M+1, M+2 isotope peaks) = Mr. Fragmentation: loss of groups gives fragment peaks. Common losses: −15 (CH₃), −29 (CHO or C₂H₅), −45 (OEt), −77 (C₆H₅). Base peak: most abundant fragment ion.

points.title: IR spectroscopy key absorptions
points.content: O–H (alcohol): broad 3230–3550 cm⁻¹. O–H (carboxylic acid): very broad 2500–3300 cm⁻¹. N–H: 3300–3500 cm⁻¹. C–H: 2850–3100 cm⁻¹. C≡N: 2200–2260 cm⁻¹. C=O (carbonyl): strong, sharp 1680–1750 cm⁻¹ (ester ~1735, aldehyde/ketone ~1715, carboxylic acid ~1710). C–O: 1050–1300 cm⁻¹. Fingerprint region: 500–1500 cm⁻¹.

points.title: ¹H NMR chemical shifts
points.content: TMS = 0 ppm reference. R–CH₃: ~0.9 ppm. R–CH₂–R: ~1.3 ppm. R–CH=: 4.5–6.5 ppm (alkene). ArH: 6.5–8.5 ppm (benzene ring). R–CHO: ~9–10 ppm (aldehyde). R–COOH: ~10–12 ppm (carboxylic acid). R–OH: 1–5 ppm (variable). NH: 1–5 ppm. Electronegative groups shift nearby H downfield (+).

points.title: NMR spin-spin coupling
points.content: (n+1) rule: a proton with n equivalent neighbouring protons is split into (n+1) peaks. Doublet (d): 1 neighbour. Triplet (t): 2 neighbours. Quartet (q): 3 neighbours. Singlet (s): 0 neighbours. Integration gives relative number of each type of H. D₂O shake: exchangeable H (OH, NH) disappear.

points.title: Combining spectroscopic data
points.content: Strategy: 1. Find Mr from mass spectrum. 2. Calculate degrees of unsaturation: DoU = (2C + 2 + N − H − X)/2. 3. IR: identify functional groups (C=O, OH, NH). 4. ¹H NMR: count types of H, integration, coupling pattern. 5. Piece together consistent structure.

points.title: Chromatography types
points.content: TLC (thin layer): stationary = silica, mobile = solvent. Rf = distance spot / distance solvent. GC: stationary = liquid on support, mobile = inert carrier gas; retention time identifies compound; used with MS for identification. HPLC: liquid mobile phase, high pressure; separates polar/ionic compounds. Paper chromatography: water in cellulose fibres is stationary phase.

points.title: Chromatography principles: mobile and stationary phases
points.content: Principle: mobile phase (solvent or inert gas) moves past stationary phase (solid or non-volatile liquid on inert support). Components separated based on relative affinity for each phase. TLC: stationary = Al₂O₃/SiO₂ (adsorption), mobile = solvent; Rf = distance of spot/distance of solvent front. GC: retention time determined by interaction strength with stationary phase (stronger interaction = longer retention) and solubility/volatility in mobile phase (greater solubility = shorter retention).

points.title: NMR practical: TMS, solvents, and D₂O exchange
points.content: TMS (tetramethylsilane, Si(CH₃)₄): used as chemical shift reference standard, δ = 0 ppm. CDCl₃: polar deuterated solvent, produces no signal in ¹H NMR. CCl₄: nonpolar solvent alternative. D₂O shake: identifies exchangeable protons (–OH, –NH). Proton exchange: –OH + D₂O ⇌ –OD + HOD, causing –OH/NH signal to disappear from spectrum.
